entities.summary:
Domenico Maria Novara da Ferrara (born 1454, died August 25, 1504) was a prominent Italian astronomer and mathematician of the late Quattrocento, recognized for his critical engagement with Ptolemaic cosmology and his influential role as a mentor to Nicolaus Copernicus. Operating primarily from Bologna, Novara's work contributed to the intellectual ferment that characterized Renaissance astronomy, challenging established geocentric views and laying groundwork for future heliocentric theories. His significance lies not only in his own observational work but critically in shaping the early scientific outlook of one of history's most revolutionary thinkers, thereby indirectly contributing to the Copernican Revolution.

Appointed Professor of Astronomy at the University of Bologna in 1483, Novara dedicated himself to meticulous astronomical observations, often critiquing the accuracy of Ptolemy's *Almagest*. Between 1489 and 1500, he compiled a catalogue of observations, including several lunar occultations and planetary conjunctions, which revealed discrepancies with prevailing Ptolemaic models. Notably, on March 9, 1497, he observed a lunar occultation of Aldebaran alongside his student, Copernicus, an event that likely reinforced their shared skepticism about the existing astronomical framework. His published work, *Calendarium Novarae*, while not a theoretical treatise, demonstrated his practical expertise and commitment to observational astronomy.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Novara's meticulous observations and critical approach to astronomy directly influenced Nicolaus Copernicus, laying crucial groundwork for the heliocentric model. His role as Copernicus's mentor ensured that his emphasis on empirical data and questioning received global intellectual resonance.
